CSET485 – AI and Society: Assignment #1 (10 Marks)

Algorithmic Stress-Testing, Hidden Confounds & Fairness Trade-Offs in Credit Underwriting
Enrollment ID: s24bcau0154
Dataset: German Credit Data (Statlog)
Seed: 154 (Last 3 digits)
Partition: 70% Train (700) / 30% Test (300)
Target: Approval (1=Approve, 0=Reject)
Code: Reproducible Jupyter Notebook

Objective: High-stakes predictive algorithms in credit lending frequently appear statistically sound while concealing demographic disparities, severe omitted-variable bias, and irreconcilable fairness trade-offs. Using the German Credit dataset (N=1,000), this report stress-tests Linear OLS and Logistic Regression across threshold mismatches, Simpson's paradox, omitted-variable bias, adversarial failure clusters, and parametric fairness frontiers. All conclusions directly reference our computed numbers.

Data Preprocessing & Exploratory Audit

1. Missing Values: Verified exactly 0 missing values across all 1,000 instances and 20 features, conforming to documentation.

2. Categorical Encoding: 13 qualitative features (checking status, credit history, purpose, savings, employment, housing, etc.) were encoded via One-Hot Encoding dropping the first category (drop_first=True) to avoid multicollinearity and dummy variable traps, yielding 41 indicator columns and 7 continuous regressors (48 total modeled predictors).

3. Feature Scaling: Standardized all 7 continuous features (duration, credit_amount, installment_commitment, residence_since, age, existing_credits, num_dependents) using StandardScaler fit strictly on the 70% training split (N=700, seed=154) to eliminate data leakage.

4. Outlier Rationale: Identified 70 outliers in duration (7.0%), 72 in credit_amount (7.2%), and 23 in age (2.3%) via the 1.5 × IQR rule. These were deliberately preserved without clipping; high balances and long maturities represent legitimate tail-risk default liabilities that underwriting models must learn.

Part 1 — Model Fitting & Threshold Mismatch Analysis

Both models were fitted on the identical 700-sample training matrix (train approval base rate: 69.71%, test base rate: 70.67%):

  • Model A (Linear OLS Regression): Continuous predictions Y_hat on the test set range from -0.0211 to 1.3459 with an empirical median of 0.7151. Thresholding at median (Y_hat ≥ 0.7151) classifies exactly 150 instances (50.0%) as positive.
  • Model B (Logistic Regression): Sigmoidal probabilities P_hat range in [0.0628, 0.9946]. Thresholding at standard P_hat ≥ 0.50 classifies 240 instances (80.0%) as positive. Test accuracy: Model B = 75.33% vs. Model A = 68.00%.

Mechanism: Exactly 90 out of 300 individuals (30.00%) are mismatched. Model A forces a relative rank median split (50/50), rejecting qualified borrowers in the corridor 0.5000 ≤ P_hat_B < 0.7151, while Model B reflects the true 70.67% base rate.

Part 2.1 — Simpson's Paradox Hunt

Stress-testing parameter stability across demographic cohorts uncovered two major instances of Simpson's Paradox and subgroup heterogeneity:

1. Sign Reversal on Existing Credits across Age: In the full population (N=1,000), bivariate logistic regression indicates that existing credits increase approval odds (β = +0.1780). Disaggregating by age reveals an acute sign reversal: for Young Adults (<30, N=371), the coefficient reverses to negative (β = -0.2203), while for Mature Adults (≥30, N=629), it is strongly positive (β = +0.3083, p = 0.0519). For young borrowers, multiple loans signal emergency borrowing and liquidity distress; for mature adults, they reflect established credit history.

2. Age Divergence across Gender: In standardized multivariable regression, applicant age has zero statistical impact on men (β_Male = +0.0604, p = 0.5204), but acts as an enormous protective factor for women (β_Female = +0.4741, p = 0.0013)—an effect size nearly eight times larger.

Part 2.2 — Omitted-Variable Bias (OVB) Stress-Testing

To measure vulnerability to hidden confounding, checking_status (Attribute 1: checking account liquidity) was deliberately purged. Because liquidity is correlated with savings reserves and employment stability, remaining regressors absorbed the omitted explanatory power via proxy correlation: E[beta_hat] = beta_true + beta_omitted × Cov(X, Z)/Var(X).

Part 2.3 — Adversarial Subset Construction & Failure Mechanics

On the test set (N=300), we extracted cases where Model B made confident errors (P_hat ≥ 0.75 with default Y=0, or P_hat ≤ 0.25 with approval Y=1). Exactly 24 instances (8.00% of test cohort) satisfied this condition: 21 high-confidence false positives, 3 high-confidence false negatives.

Table 4: Adversarial Failures vs. Test Baseline Profile

Metric / Characteristic Test Baseline (N=300) Adversarial (N=24) Disparity Signature
Homeownership (housing = A152) 74.00% 83.33% +9.33% Over-Represented
Moderate Checking (A12: 0–200 DM) 23.00% 45.83% Nearly Double Baseline (+22.83%)
Clean Credit History (A32) 53.67% 54.17% Parity with Clean Baseline
Mean Requested Loan Amount 3,040.18 DM 3,337.50 DM +$297.32 DM Heavier Burden
Female Representation 28.33% 20.83% -7.50% Under-Represented

Failure Mechanics: Logistic regression assumes linear additivity: z = sum(beta_i * X_i). The model summed positive weights for homeownership (+0.283) and moderate checking (+0.345), ignoring the non-linear interaction between loan size and liquidity (credit_amount * checking_status). A 200 DM buffer cushions small loans, but fails against a 3,337.50 DM debt.

Part 3 — Descriptive Analysis (Questions 1, 2 & 3)

Question 1: Comparative Classification Dynamics & Mismatch Mechanics 260 words

In our test set evaluation (N=300), Model A (Linear OLS) and Model B (Logistic Regression) generated exactly 90 mismatched cases (30.00% mismatch rate). Model A continuous predictions ranged from -0.0211 to 1.3459 with an empirical test set median of 0.7151. Mandating the threshold at the median forces exactly 50.0% of the sample (N=150) into positive approval by construction. In contrast, Model B maps log-odds through the logistic sigmoid link function, producing valid posterior probabilities strictly bounded in [0.0628, 0.9946]. Applying the standard cutoff P_hat ≥ 0.50 classified 240 individuals (80.00%) into positive approval. The inter-model confusion matrix confirms the structural nature of this disagreement: both models agreed on 60 negative and 150 positive classifications, while exactly 90 individuals were approved by Model B (P_hat ≥ 0.50) but rejected by Model A (Y_hat < 0.7151), with 0 approved by Model A and rejected by Model B.

This 30% mismatch stems from diverging thresholding philosophies. Model A’s median split is a relative, rank-based ordinal threshold that artificially rejects half the cohort regardless of creditworthiness. Because the test base rate is 70.67% positive, Model B’s absolute threshold (0.50) reflects the true positive skew. The 90 disputed individuals occupy the corridor 0.5000 ≤ P_hat_B < 0.7151: creditworthy applicants who are penalized solely for falling below the 50th percentile of peers. OLS also extrapolates outside probability bounds (-0.0211 and 1.3459). Consequently, Model B achieved 75.33% test accuracy vs. Model A’s 68.00%.

Question 2: Simpson's Paradox and Subgroup Heterogeneity 265 words

We uncovered an acute instance of Simpson’s Paradox when analyzing the impact of existing bank credit lines (existing_credits) across age cohorts: Young Adults (<30 years, N=371) vs. Mature Adults (≥30 years, N=629). In the full population (N=1,000), bivariate logistic regression indicates that existing credits positively predict approval (β_Full = +0.1780, SE = 0.1232, p = 0.1488, 95% CI: [-0.0636, +0.4195]). However, disaggregating by age reveals an acute sign reversal:

  • Young Adults (<30 years): β_Young = -0.2203 (SE = 0.2133, p = 0.3016, 95% CI: [-0.6384, +0.1977]) — Negative Penalty
  • Mature Adults (≥30 years): β_Mature = +0.3083 (SE = 0.1586, p = 0.0519, 95% CI: [-0.0025, +0.6192]) — Positive Asset

Statistically, this reversal reflects distinct latent behavioral meanings across life stages. For mature adults, multiple credit accounts indicate an established track record and banking trust. For young adults, multiple loans signal financial instability, over-leveraging, and emergency liquidity distress. Furthermore, in standardized multivariable regression, applicant age has zero statistical impact on men (β_Male = +0.0604, p = 0.5204), but acts as an enormous protective factor for women (β_Female = +0.4741, p = 0.0013)—an effect size nearly eight times larger. Deploying an aggregate model that ignores these subgroup interactions would reward over-indebted young borrowers while mispricing young women.

Question 3: Omitted-Variable Bias (OVB) Stress-Testing 250 words

We deliberately omitted checking_status (Attribute 1: checking liquidity) from the full logistic regression model (48 features, N=700) to measure parameter sensitivity to unobserved confounds. The resulting coefficient shifts confirm severe omitted-variable bias:

The predictor that shifted most was savings_status_A63 (+110.00%), followed by employment_A73 (+100.31%). Because checking liquidity is positively correlated with savings and stable employment, purging checking status forced the optimizer to inflate savings and employment weights through proxy absorption: E[beta_hat] = beta_true + beta_omitted × Cov(X, Z)/Var(X). An auditor inspecting the reduced model would falsely attribute double the true protective effect to moderate savings, demonstrating that un-stress-tested models cannot be trusted for causal underwriting explanations.

Part 3 — Descriptive Analysis (Questions 4, 5, 6 & 7)

Question 4: Detecting Hidden Confounds in Production Systems 230 words

In enterprise lending, unobserved confounders (such as family safety nets or informal remittances) bias training and test sets identically. To detect them, I propose a dual-track strategy combining Quasi-Experimental Instrumental Variable (IV) Estimation with Oster Sensitivity Bounding. (1) We exploit hyper-local banking competition shocks (e.g., staggered regional branch rollouts or postal-code banking fee reforms) as an exogenous instrument (Z). Because branch competition affects loan terms and checking account uptake without altering an applicant's intrinsic moral hazard, it satisfies relevance and exclusion restrictions. A Hausman test comparing beta_OLS against beta_IV formally tests for omitted confounding. (2) We compute Oster's proportionality delta relative to movements in R^2; delta < 1.0 indicates fragility to selection on unobservables. Finally, a negative control outcome (applicant telephone registration) is audited: non-zero weights prove socio-economic confounding.

Question 5: Adversarial Subset Construction & Failure Mechanics 240 words

We identified exactly 24 adversarial failure instances (8.00% of the 300 test subjects): 21 high-confidence false positives (P_hat ≥ 0.75, true default) and 3 high-confidence false negatives (P_hat ≤ 0.25, true approved). Profiling reveals striking shared traits: 83.33% own their homes (vs. 74.00% test baseline), 45.83% hold moderate checking accounts (0–200 DM) (nearly double the 23.00% baseline), 54.17% have clean credit histories, and their average loan obligation was 3,337.50 DM (vs. 3,040.18 DM baseline). Logistic regression failed confidently due to linear additivity without non-linear interaction terms: it summed positive weights for homeownership (+0.283) and checking status (+0.345), ignoring that a modest 200 DM reserve cannot service an above-average 3,337.50 DM debt obligation.

Question 6: The Real-World Cost of Fairness Trade-Offs 250 words

Consider two realistic applicants: Elena (Female, 28, P_hat = 0.480) seeking a 2,500 DM catering equipment loan, and Marcus (Male, 29, P_hat = 0.480) seeking an identical auto repair loan. Under an Inclusion Threshold (t = 0.35), both exceed the threshold and receive loans; Demographic Parity is high (DP = 0.9292, Female approval = 84.71%, Male approval = 91.16%) and Equalized Odds is robust (EO = 0.8108, TPR_Female = 93.22%, TPR_Male = 95.42%). However, under an Accuracy-Maximizing Threshold (t = 0.55), both Elena and Marcus are rejected (0.480 < 0.55). Female approval collapses to 68.24% and EO collapses to 0.5156. If a regulator demands perfect DP (1.000) at t=0.55, the bank would have to set disparate thresholds (t_female = 0.45, t_male = 0.55), approving Elena while rejecting Marcus despite identical 0.480 risk scores, violating individual fairness.

Question 7: Defending an Operational Decision Threshold (t = 0.35) 255 words

I defend t = 0.35 as the optimal operational threshold based on four empirical metrics: (1) Demographic Parity = 0.9292 (Female approval 84.71%, Male approval 91.16%), satisfying the EEOC 80% rule; (2) Equalized Odds = 0.8108, with true positive parity at 0.9769 (TPR_Female = 93.22% vs. TPR_Male = 95.42%); (3) Predictive Parity = 1.0255 (PPV_Female = 76.39% vs. PPV_Male = 74.49%); and (4) Accuracy = 74.00% (only 2.33% below peak 76.33% at t=0.55). Strongest Counter-Argument: A credit officer will argue that t=0.35 elevates the False Positive Rate to 65.38% for women and 80.65% for men, approving 67 defaulting applicants in a 5:1 cost matrix. This valid credit risk must be managed via risk-adjusted loan pricing and tiered borrowing caps rather than demographic exclusion.

Part 3 (Cont.) — Question 8 & Part 4 Reflection Essay

Question 8: Strategic Policy Choice: Demographic Parity vs. Equalized Odds 235 words

If forced to choose, I unequivocally recommend prioritizing Equalized Odds (EO) over pure Demographic Parity (DP). Under Kleinberg’s Impossibility Theorem, unequal base rates (Female 69.41% vs. Male 71.16%) make DP, EO, and PP mutually incompatible. Equalized Odds enforces meritocratic fairness: creditworthy applicants face equal approval odds regardless of sex (at t=0.35, TPR_Female = 93.22% vs. TPR_Male = 95.42%, a 2.20% gap), while preserving Predictive Parity (PP = 1.0255). We explicitly sacrifice strict DP (0.9292 at t=0.35; 0.8480 at t=0.55). Sacrificing pure DP is necessary: enforcing equal acceptance rates across unequal financial distributions would force banks to approve unqualified women (causing debt traps and default) or deny qualified men, violating procedural justice.

Part 4 — Reflection Essay (~470 words)

"If a policy-maker asked you: 'just give me one number: should we deploy this model or not?', what would you say, and what is the limitation of that 'one number' answer that you discovered yourself through your analysis?"
1. Direct Answer (1–2 sentences) ~35 words

I recommend conditional deployment under strict segment-specific thresholding (t = 0.35) and continuous human-in-the-loop oversight, because a single binary deployment number obscures that default thresholding maximizes global accuracy while destroying equal opportunity for female borrowers and failing predictably on high-exposure homeowners.

2. Why a Single Number Fails (300–400 words) ~325 words

The fundamental lesson of this stress-test audit is that reducing a sociotechnical AI system to a single summary metric—whether overall accuracy (75.33%), AUC-ROC (0.792), or a composite index—is an act of intellectual complacency that conceals severe structural trade-offs.

First, aggregate accuracy systematically masks catastrophic subgroup collapses. At our model’s peak accuracy threshold of t = 0.55 (76.33% accuracy), Equalized Odds collapses to a dismal 0.5156, with the model approving non-creditworthy men at nearly double the rate of non-creditworthy women (FPR_Male = 59.68% vs. FPR_Female = 30.77%), while female loan approvals plunge to 68.24%. Celebrating "76% accuracy" ignores that half of the equal opportunity metric has been eliminated.

Second, threshold selection is an unstated value judgment, not a mathematical fact. Choosing between t = 0.35 (prioritizing inclusion and EO of 0.8108) and t = 0.55 (prioritizing default suppression and bank profitability) cannot be answered by data science. It is an economic and political choice balancing borrower credit access against institutional capital loss. Collapsing this to a binary "deploy" command abdicates human accountability to an arbitrary mathematical default (0.50).

Third, fairness metrics are mathematically adversarial. Under Kleinberg's and Chouldechova's theorems, differing base default rates (69.41% female vs. 71.16% male) ensure that Demographic Parity, Equalized Odds, and Predictive Parity cannot be simultaneously fulfilled. Gaining +4.27% in DP from t=0.75 to t=0.85 causes EO to plunge -24.99%—a punishing trade-off cost ratio of 5.85. A single metric conceals which protected group is paying the cost.

Fourth, models fail with extreme confidence on predictable adversarial clusters. Our model confidently misclassified 24 test cases (8.00%), assigning P_hat ≥ 0.75 to defaulting applicants simply because they were homeowners (83.33%) with moderate checking reserves (45.83%), oblivious to their heavy 3,337.50 DM debt burden.

Finally, hidden confounds remain invisible to summary statistics. Purging checking liquidity caused savings weights to inflate by +110.00% and employment weights by +100.31%, proving that observational models readily disguise omitted confounders as legitimate risk indicators.

3. Grounding in Evidence (50–100 words) ~60 words

Our computations substantiate every limitation: the 30.00% mismatch between Model A and B, the Simpson’s sign reversal on existing credits (-0.2203 young vs. +0.3083 mature), the 110.00% coefficient inflation under omitted-variable testing, the 24 adversarial failures with 83.33% homeownership, and the plunge in Equalized Odds from 0.8108 at t=0.35 to 0.5156 at t=0.55.

4. Closing (50 words) ~45 words

Responsible AI governance is an exercise in transparently navigating unavoidable trade-offs, not chasing single-metric optimization. A single number offers executives the illusion of certainty; true algorithmic accountability demands exposing who wins, who loses, and which ethical values are compromised at every operational threshold.
